procedural_history.originating_court: Metropolitan Magistrate, Railway Mobile Court, Andheri, Mumbai (trial court)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 26th April 2021, passed by the High Court of Judicature at Bombay and the order dated 22nd March 2017 passed by the trial court
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Appellants filed Criminal Writ Petition Nos. 348, 349 and 357 of 2020 in the High Court seeking quashing of the order dated 22nd March 2017 passed by the trial court. The High Court dismissed these petitions. The complainant/respondent No.1 filed Criminal Writ Petition Nos. 127, 128, 129 and 130 of 2020, which the High Court allowed, thereby upholding the order dated 22nd March 2017.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's judgment and order dated 26th April 2021. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, quashing the High Court's judgment and the trial court's order.

directions: The impugned judgment dated 26th April 2021 passed by the High Court and the order dated 22nd March 2017 passed by the trial court are quashed and set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the allegation that the appellants delayed the sale of pledged shares from the first default in May 2000 until August-September 2001, during which time the shares depreciated in value, could form the basis of a criminal proceeding.

facts: The complainant defaulted on a loan in May 2000.
The appellants (lenders) held shares pledged by the complainant as security.
The complainant alleged that the appellants should have sold the pledged shares at the time of the first default in May 2000.
The appellants waited until August-September 2001 to sell the shares, by which time the shares had depreciated in value.
This specific issue of delayed sale was already raised by the complainant in separate arbitration proceedings that began in 2001.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the dispute over the timing of the sale of pledged shares was "purely contractual" in nature.
The Court noted that this exact issue was already the subject of arbitration proceedings, which reinforced its character as a civil, not criminal, matter.
The Court found there was an "inordinate delay" in lodging the criminal complaint. The complainant was aware of the sale in 2001 but waited until 2011 to file the complaint.

This delay, coupled with the contractual nature of the dispute, led the Court to conclude that the complainant was attempting to turn a civil dispute into a criminal case, which it deemed an "abuse of process of law."
The Court held that the complaint, taken at face value, did not disclose the necessary ingredients to make out a criminal offense.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the allegation as a basis for a criminal proceeding because it considered the matter a purely contractual dispute that was already being addressed in arbitration. The Court also found that the inordinate ten-year delay in filing the criminal complaint constituted an abuse of the legal process.

issue.issue_text: Whether the contention that the pledged shares were sold at a price lesser than the prevailing market price has any substance.

facts: The claimant sold the pledged shares at an average price of Rs. 2.47 per share.
The average market price around that time was Rs. 2.95 per share.
The complainant had defaulted on the loan, which constrained the claimant to sell the entire security.
The Letter of Pledge (LoP) signed by the complainant explicitly stated that they would not question whether the claimant (pledgee) had obtained the best price for the securities.
The share sale transactions were conducted through the official stock exchanges, the BSE and NSE.
law: A clause in the Letter of Pledge (LoP) contractually barred the complainant (pledgor) from questioning the price at which the pledged shares were sold.
application: The Court found the difference between the sale price (Rs. 2.47) and the market price (Rs. 2.95) to be a "marginal fluctuation."

This marginal difference was not considered evidence of price manipulation, especially given that the claimant was forced to sell due to the complainant's "habitual default" and there were not many buyers.
The Court emphasized that the complainant had contractually agreed in the LoP not to challenge the sale price obtained by the claimant.
The fact that the sales were executed through official stock exchanges (BSE and NSE) further weakened the claim of an improper sale.
The Court also noted that the allegation was not properly made in the original complaint.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the contention that the shares were sold for less than the market price, finding it to be without substance. The Court reasoned that the price difference was marginal, the complainant was contractually barred from making such a claim by the Letter of Pledge, and the sales were conducted properly through the stock exchanges.

appellant_arguments: The delay in selling pledged shares, even if it resulted in a loss of value, is a civil dispute and cannot be the basis for a criminal proceeding. (Inferred from the issue as the appellant's specific arguments are not detailed in the text)

arguments.issue_text: Whether the contention that the pledged shares were sold at a price lesser than the prevailing market price has any substance.
appellant_arguments: The contention that the shares were sold for less than the market price lacks substance, especially as a basis for a criminal charge. (Inferred from the issue as the appellant's specific arguments are not detailed in the text)
respondent_arguments: The shares were sold at a meagre price to a company where accused Nos. 2 and 3 are also Directors.
This sale at a low price to an affiliated company clearly exhibits a dishonest intention on the part of the appellants.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A contention within a criminal complaint is without substance if there is no averment in the complaint regarding that specific contention, and a finding on the matter has already been made by an arbitrator in an award that is currently under challenge in a competent court.
obiter: Nothing observed in the judgment should influence the forum handling the arbitral award proceedings under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act or any other related legal proceedings.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found that the criminal complaint, when taken at face value, does not disclose the necessary ingredients of the offenses alleged. The dispute is governed by a Letter of Pledge which specifically authorized the appellants to sell the shares and contained a clause where the respondent agreed not to question the price obtained. Therefore, the criminal proceeding is an abuse of the process of law.
legal_tests_applied: Whether the complaint, taken at its face value, discloses that any of the ingredients of the offence complained of have been made out.
why_appellant_lost: The respondent's arguments were rejected because the Letter of Pledge, which the respondent had agreed to, explicitly gave the appellants the authority to sell the shares to adjust the outstanding amount.

The respondent's central contention—that the shares were sold at a low price—was contractually barred, as the agreement stated the respondent would not 'dispute or claim any loss on account of price at which securities are sold by the lender'.
why_respondent_won: The appellants' position was accepted because their actions were governed by sub-clause (v) of Clause 8 of the Letter of Pledge, which provided them with the authority to sell the pledged securities.

The Court found that the respondent had contractually waived the right to question the sale price of the securities, which undermined the entire basis of the criminal complaint alleging a fraudulent sale.
The Court concluded that the complaint failed to make out the essential ingredients of a criminal offense, particularly any dishonest intention, as the actions taken were contractually permitted.
policy_considerations: The Court found that the criminal complaint was 'nothing else but an abuse of process of law,' reinforcing the policy that the criminal justice system should not be used to settle disputes that are fundamentally civil and contractual in nature.
